note: Row = [symbol, name, atomic mass, category, state at 25 C, display colour, Pauling electronegativity, common oxidation states (first = most common), flags (R radioactive, S superheavy: only atoms ever made), fact]. Atomic number = row index + 1. Interim content - needs reviewer sign-off.
elements: Hydrogen is the most abundant element in the universe - about three quarters of all normal matter.
Helium was discovered in the Sun's light before anyone found it on Earth.
Lithium is so light it floats on oil, and it powers most rechargeable batteries.
Beryllium lets X-rays straight through, so it is used for X-ray tube windows.
Boron compounds give fireworks a bright green colour.
Diamond and graphite are both pure carbon - the atoms are just arranged differently.
Nitrogen makes up 78% of the air you breathe.
Liquid oxygen is pale blue and is attracted to magnets.
Fluorine is the most reactive element of all - it even attacks glass.
Neon glows red-orange in electric signs.
Sodium is soft enough to cut with a knife and is stored under oil to keep air and water away.
Magnesium burns with a dazzling white light that was once used for camera flashes.
Aluminium is the most abundant metal in Earth's crust, but it was once more valuable than gold.
Silicon is at the heart of every computer chip.
Phosphorus was discovered in 1669 by an alchemist boiling down urine.
Sulfur burns with a blue flame; volcanoes release huge amounts of it.
Chlorine keeps swimming pools and drinking water free of germs.
Almost 1% of the air around you is argon.
Potassium reacts with water so fast that the hydrogen bursts into a lilac flame.
Your bones and teeth are built from calcium compounds.
Scandium is added to aluminium to make light, strong bike frames.
Titanium is as strong as steel but about 45% lighter.
Vanadium compounds show four different colours - one for each oxidation state.
Chromium gives rubies their red and emeralds their green.
Manganese is essential for making tough steel.
Earth's core is mostly iron - and so is the haemoglobin carrying oxygen in your blood.
Cobalt blue has been used to colour glass and pottery for thousands of years.
Despite its name, a US 'nickel' coin is mostly copper.
The Statue of Liberty is green because its copper skin has corroded.
A coat of zinc stops steel from rusting - this is called galvanising.
Gallium melts at 29.8 C - it would melt in your hand.
Mendeleev predicted germanium's properties 15 years before it was discovered.
Arsenic is a famous historical poison.
Selenium conducts electricity better in light, which made early photocopiers work.
Bromine is one of only two elements that are liquid at room temperature.
Kryptonite is fictional, but krypton is real and glows white in lamps.
Rubidium is used in atomic clocks.
Strontium salts give fireworks their crimson red.
Yttrium made the red colour in old colour TV screens.
Cubic zirconia, a diamond look-alike, is zirconium oxide.
Niobium alloys make the superconducting magnets inside MRI scanners.
Molybdenum melts at 2623 C, so it is used in furnace parts.
Technetium was the first element made artificially, in 1937.
A little ruthenium makes platinum jewellery harder.
Rhodium is one of the most expensive metals on Earth.
Palladium can soak up 900 times its own volume of hydrogen gas.
Silver conducts electricity and heat better than any other element.
Cadmium makes bright yellow paint pigments, but it is toxic.
Indium tin oxide makes touch screens work.
'Tin' cans are really steel with a thin coat of tin.
Ancient Egyptians used antimony compounds as eye make-up.
Tellurium is used in rewritable DVDs and solar panels.
Heated iodine turns straight from shiny crystals into a violet vapour.
In 1962 xenon became the first noble gas shown to form compounds.
One second is defined by counting vibrations of caesium atoms.
A 'barium meal' makes your gut show up on X-rays.
Lanthanum is used in high-quality camera lenses.
Lighter 'flints' contain cerium - it sparks when scratched.
Praseodymium tints welders' goggles to block harsh yellow light.
Neodymium makes the strongest permanent magnets, found in headphones and wind turbines.
Promethium was once used in glow-in-the-dark watch paint.
Samarium-cobalt magnets survive very high temperatures.
Europium makes euro banknotes glow red under UV light.
Gadolinium helps doctors see clearer MRI scans.
Terbium gives the green colour in energy-saving lamps.
Dysprosium's name means 'hard to get at' in Greek.
Holmium has the highest magnetic strength of any element.
Erbium boosts the light signals in fibre-optic internet cables.
Thulium is one of the rarest naturally occurring lanthanides.
Ytterbium is named after Ytterby, a Swedish village that gave its name to four elements.
Lutetium crystals detect radiation in PET body scanners.
Hafnium soaks up neutrons, so it is used in nuclear reactor control rods.
Almost every mobile phone contains tantalum capacitors.
Tungsten has the highest melting point of any metal: 3422 C.
Rhenium, found in 1925, was one of the last stable elements discovered.
Osmium is the densest naturally occurring element.
A thin layer of iridium in rocks marks the asteroid impact that ended the dinosaurs.
Car catalytic converters use platinum to clean exhaust gases.
Gold is so unreactive that ancient gold jewellery is still shiny after thousands of years.
Mercury is the only metal that is liquid at room temperature.
Thallium is highly toxic and was once used as rat poison.
The word 'plumbing' comes from plumbum, Latin for lead - Romans made water pipes from it.
Bismuth crystals grow as rainbow-coloured staircases.
Polonium was discovered by Marie Curie and named after her home country, Poland.
Less than 30 grams of astatine exists in Earth's crust at any moment.
Radon is a radioactive gas that can build up in basements.
Francium is so radioactive that nobody has ever seen a visible piece of it.
Radium glows faintly in the dark and was discovered by Marie and Pierre Curie.
Actinium glows pale blue in the dark.
Thorium was once used in gas-lantern mantles to make a bright white light.
Protactinium is one of the rarest naturally occurring elements.
Uranium is the fuel for nuclear power stations.
Neptunium is named after Neptune, the planet after Uranus.
Heat from plutonium has powered space probes like Voyager for decades.
A tiny speck of americium sits inside most smoke detectors.
Curium is named after Marie and Pierre Curie.
Berkelium is named after Berkeley, California, where it was made.
Californium is used to start up nuclear reactors.
Einsteinium was first found in the debris of the first hydrogen bomb test.
Fermium is named after physicist Enrico Fermi.
Mendelevium honours Dmitri Mendeleev, who created the periodic table.
Nobelium is named after Alfred Nobel, founder of the Nobel Prizes.
Lawrencium honours Ernest Lawrence, inventor of the cyclotron.
Rutherfordium is named after Ernest Rutherford, who discovered the atomic nucleus.
Dubnium is named after Dubna, a Russian science city.
Seaborgium was named after Glenn Seaborg while he was still alive.
Bohrium honours Niels Bohr, a pioneer of atomic structure.
Hassium is named after the German state of Hesse.
Meitnerium honours Lise Meitner, who helped explain nuclear fission.
Darmstadtium is named after the German city of Darmstadt.
Roentgenium honours Wilhelm Roentgen, discoverer of X-rays.
Copernicium is named after astronomer Nicolaus Copernicus.
Nihonium was the first element discovered in Asia, in Japan.
Flerovium is named after the Flerov nuclear physics laboratory.
Moscovium is named after the Moscow region.
Livermorium is named after the Lawrence Livermore laboratory.
Tennessine is named after the US state of Tennessee.
Oganesson is the heaviest element known - only five or six atoms have ever been made.
